title: I am someone else (2:4)
hookLine: the returner cries out, gives, keeps away from the cause, even changes name and deeds
tomorrow: is a private sorry enough when others heard the wrong?

cards: You haven't changed a bit. At a reunion, it's a compliment. After a fight, it's a verdict.
So can a person actually become someone else? Maimonides says yes, and he lists the ways. The returner cries out before God, with tears and pleading.

Gives tzedakah, as much as they're able. Keeps far away from the thing that tripped them. And then two surprises: they change their deeds, all of them, toward the good, and they may even change their name.

teach.h: NOT THE ONE WHO DID THOSE THINGS.
teach.b: Why a name? Maimonides gives the returner's own words: as if to say, I am someone else, not the one who did those things. He even adds leaving home for a while, exile, as part of the turn.

Here's the best case for this view: change needs room. A new name, a new street, new habits give the new person somewhere to stand, so the old one isn't waiting on every corner. Now the other voice, from the Talmud.
Reish Lakish says return is so great that deliberate sins become like merits, when the return comes from love. In a Talmud story, Reish Lakish himself had lived as a bandit before he turned to study.
On this view, the past isn't shed like a coat. It becomes fuel.
The one who did it is exactly the one who now knows better, and the history is put to work. Its best case: you can't help the next person climb out of a hole you pretend you were never in.
So one voice says: I am someone else now. The other says: I'm the same person, and that's why this counts. Both are inside the tradition, and both agree on one thing.

how: Some Jews study these ways of return in the days before Yom Kippur, when giving tzedakah and asking people for forgiveness are part of the season for some families.

games.q: what does “i am someone else” mean?
o: a mask an actor wears to play a new role
a convert's new name given at a ceremony
the returner's words: not the one who did it

games.q: the ways of return — tap the pairs.
p: before God, with tears and pleading
give, as much as you're able
from the thing that tripped you

s: in Judaism, a person who did wrong is stuck with being that person
Maimonides lists ways to change, down to the returner saying: I am someone else.
a Talmud sage says deliberate sins can become like merits
Reish Lakish: when return comes from love.
Maimonides says a new name is required before return counts
it's one of several ways he lists; the change that counts is in the deeds.

games.q: your friend Owen says changing your name after doing wrong is just running from it. what's Maimonides' best case back?
o: a new name gives new deeds room: I am someone else, not the one who did it.
a new name hides the past, so nobody can ever hold it against you.
a new name is the whole of return; once it's changed, the rest follows.
games.why: Maimonides pairs the name with changed deeds. and Owen's worry has a voice inside the tradition too: Reish Lakish keeps the past and puts it to work.

practice: Choose one small thing you'd like to be different about you this week. Name the wish, then the one obstacle most likely to get in its way.
Then make a plan in a single sentence, if this happens, then I'll do that, and rest with it until the bell.

wordCard.voice: I am someone else: the returner's words in Maimonides, not the one who did those things. Said with new deeds, and sometimes a new name.

orig.note: Hebrew: I am another, the returner's words in Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:4.

carryVoice: Carry this one: I am someone else now, or, if you lean the other way, the same someone, turned. Day fifteen forty-three.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:4 (crying out, charity, keeping away, a changed name, changed deeds, exile)
Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 86b (Reish Lakish: return from love turns deliberate sins into merits)
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 84a (Reish Lakish's life before study)
